lines.text: Two small islands in the eastern Caribbean, shaped by sugar and slavery, then by freedom, independence and cricket. This is Antigua and Barbuda.
English settlers arrived in 1632 and built sugar plantations worked by enslaved Africans. The town of St John's grew into their capital and port.
At English Harbour, the Royal Navy built a dockyard that still stands, now a World Heritage Site named after Horatio Nelson.
In 1833 Britain passed a law to end slavery. The owners were paid, and the freed people got nothing.
Vere Bird was born. He would lead the labour movement, win self-rule, and become the country's first prime minister.
In St John's, Jamaica Kincaid was born, a novelist who would write sharply about her island in A Small Place.
Then came the cricketers. Andy Roberts, a fast bowler, became the first Antiguan to play Test cricket for the West Indies.
A year after him came Viv Richards, who would lead the great West Indies side and hit the fastest bowlers without a helmet.
Curtly Ambrose followed, a towering fast bowler who took more than four hundred Test wickets.
Gaston Browne was born, a future prime minister who would take office in 2014.
That year Antigua became one of the West Indies Associated States, governing itself, a step on the road to independence.
In 1981, after three and a half centuries of British rule, Antigua and Barbuda became an independent nation.
In 2017 Hurricane Irma wrecked almost every building on Barbuda, and the whole island had to be emptied.
From sugar fields to cricket grounds, these two small islands have made a big mark on the world.
